This significant improvement is a direct result of the inherent properties of the generated graph topology, which enables it to capture and utilize long-range correlations in the underlying graph structure.

The Slim Sidon sets are defined as a subset of $\mathbb{Z}_p^d$ called Slim Sidon sets, and it is proven that any vectorial Boolean mapping on $\mathbb{Z}_p^d$ to $\mathbb{Z}_p^e$ has at least a nonlinearity of $n - p^{e-1}$. Moreover, under specific conditions, it is shown that Slim Sidon sets can be used to derive lower bounds for the nonlinearity of vectorial Boolean mappings, and it is further demonstrated that our results are nearly optimal in terms of the bounds.

Binarized matrices, comprising of simple "1"-"0" pairs, are used to execute energy-efficient computations in various tasks including neural network design, data compression, and data representation. The number of possible binarized matrices is exponentially related to the size of the matrix, and determining whether a randomly selected binary matrix exhibits a specified margin property is a challenging problem. In this study, we establish the probability distribution of fixed margin binarized matrices by employing a non-uniform sampling approach. The results of our computations are then utilized to derive precise bounds on the probability of a randomly selected binary matrix having the specified margin property. The obtained bounds are found to be precise enough, with a difference of threshold h, by analyzing the binary matrix's sub-matrices and exhibiting a specified pattern. The study also explores the applicability of its findings in approximating the complexity of "NEQ BIN MAT" – a problem that involves determining whether a binary matrix has a specified minimum norm.

Introducing the uffpdf framework, a publicly-available, open-source tool for fitting PDFs to diverse datasets, with a special focus on incorporating various nuclear physics inputs from the nuclear physics community. This introductory presentation outlines the key components of the framework, highlighting its capabilities and illustrating a practical fitting process with a simple example. Furthermore, recommendations are provided for standardizing PDF fitting procedures among research groups.

This document outlines the official release of the ELKI data mining platform in version 0.7.5. Developed as an open-source initiative, the Java-based framework serves the data mining community by focusing on advanced unsupervised techniques within cluster analysis and anomaly detection. By integrating a comprehensive set of features, including background knowledge integration and efficient index-based data access, the framework aims to enhance the performance and flexibility of data mining procedures. Furthermore, the framework supports a wide range of advanced relational database management systems for more effective data mining and research purposes within statistical analysis.

We've developed an innovative technique for seeding a wide range of optical frequencies from a single mode in a microresonator. By gradually increasing the pump power in a microresonator driven by a fundamental mode, we caused a series of mode jumps that triggered the appearance of new optical modes at specific intervals. These new modes, which were equally spaced, corresponded to the gap frequency between the microresonator and the surrounding material. By aligning one of these mode jumps with a condition that the light within the microresonator naturally divides into multiple frequencies, we were able to create a array of optical frequencies with a uniform spacing. The space between these frequencies was determined by the microresonator's characteristic frequency and the nearby material's frequency. The frequency stability of these arrays, which can be used as a basis for accurate frequency measurement and comparison, was improved through the control of the pump power and the microresonator's loss levels.

We establish that every acylindrically hyperbolic group possesses a random subgroup which undergoes rapid growth, is comprised of distinct elements, and retains its "loyal" characteristics, forming a subgroup with specified properties. This finding, in turn, yields several significant conclusions, including a characterization of "weakly short" elements within any acylindrically hyperbolic group, a proof of a theory posited by Genevieve Walsh and Daniel Valle, and an extension of a concept introduced by Ilya Kapovich and Marc Lackenby.

Quantization has significant benefits of reduced storage and processing requirements for neural networks, which can also improve classification robustness to perturbations. There has been a lack of understanding about why quantization often leads to improved generalization performance. This study investigates this phenomenon through an analysis of the neural network's learning curve, using the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) model. We show that discrete binary weights in neural networks create 'obstacles' for overfitting, which are reflected in the asymmetry and irregularity of the NTK spectrum. This study also develops a method to generate binary weights that maintain the network's original functionality, which can be applied to any neural network architecture. Experimental results confirm the effectiveness of this approach in enhancing generalization performance.

Researchers have discovered a connection between quantum critical points and surfaces in higher-dimensional spaces, with a surprising finding that certain features of gravity can describe these critical phenomena more accurately than traditional theories. Notably, they found that the entropy of these quantum critical surfaces or points changes in a non-intuitive, inverted manner when cross-coupled with a parameter, now referred to as the 'hierarchy of entropies.' Instead of following a straightforward increase with system size, as predicted by the AdS/CFT correspondence, the entropy peaks at smaller system sizes and decreases at larger sizes. Recent research has revealed that this hierarchy of entropies, with its inherent asymmetry, may serve as a universal indicator of quantum critical surfaces or points in any theory, with a supercritical scenario representing the ultimate, most asymmetric form. Moreover, researchers have found that this asymmetry is mirrored in the boundary dimension, with the critical surface exhibiting more intricate characteristics than the critical point or surface. With these new insights, scientists can utilize the hierarchy of entropies to identify different dimension types, with the asymmetry indicating a quantum critical surface, point, or not being in any of these categories. Furthermore, with the hierarchy's help, researchers may be able to uncover yet unknown dimension types, with potential applications of these findings extending to materials science and other fields.

When a rigid body undergoes a snapshot transformation, we define its "configuration" as the superimposed image and its "snapshot set" as the collection of configurations resulting from various snapshot transformations applied to the body. The "intersection multiplicity" at a particular configuration refers to the greatest number of points where the snapshot sets of two distinct bodies overlap. In this research, a mathematical formula is established to calculate the intersection multiplicity for two solvable lattice frameworks using a polynomial based approach. The outcomes of this study can provide valuable insights in a variety of areas including science, art and communication.

Signal reconstruction techniques like iterative soft-thresholding or iterative hard-thresholding can be effectively used for recovering sparse signals in compressed sensing frameworks. However, convergence issues arise when trying to recover signals with non-ideal measurement processes or when incorporating prior information. In such cases, iterative stabilization methods like generalized gradient projections can be employed, offering faster convergence rates and improved stability. We examine the application of these stabilization methods to iterative reconstruction procedures and demonstrate their efficacy in achieving more robust recovery results.

We have derived expressions for the point spread functions of combined images in terms of their individual pixel values. These formulas allow for the determination of a combined image's point spread function either directly or through the calculation of its covariance matrix. This capability can be utilized to assess the overall sensitivity of a combined image or a weighted sum of images. We have further established that a weighted sum of images with weighted values $w_i \ge 0$ possesses a point spread function defined as the point spread functions' convolution with weights acting as coefficients.

Miller and Sheffield introduced the concept of an imaginary surface as a union of zero-set imaginary domains resulting from the conformal equivalence of a probability field on the upper and lower half-planes, based on the relationship between probability fields and conformal quantum mechanics. Specifically, they demonstrated that an imaginary surface associated with a given probability field is unique and stated the hypothesis that such an imaginary surface exists for Gaussian free fields with non-zero boundary conditions. Recent breakthroughs by Vintskevich and Yambur and myself, however, provide strong evidence for the existence of imaginary surfaces in Gaussian free fields with various driving mechanisms, one of which being multi-parameter SLEs. I will show that another driving mechanism, namely the multiplicative conformal central charge, also leads to the existence of imaginary surfaces. particularly in relation to critical lattice models and that this imaginary surface is closely linked to planar cluster models. Furthermore, I will derive field transformations that link Gaussian free fields to multiple SLEs driven by random log-gases. These field transformations have the beneficial effect of eliminating order parameter non-uniqueness found in conventional driving mechanisms, such as temperature or field parameter variations.

This research investigates the unique characteristics of solutions to the Cauchy problem for the Navier-Stokes equations with periodic conditions, specifically when the momentum vector has a constant magnitude and certain conditions are met. By introducing a parameter that measures solution behavior in relation to a large constant, B, our analysis determines when a unique solution exists and evaluates the time at which it occurs, ultimately expressing this time in terms of B. Unlike previous studies using statistical methods, our analysis provides a precise mathematical connection between these parameters. Furthermore, we confirm that in the limit where B approaches infinity, the time at which the solution exists converges in probability to a specific value, providing a priori estimates for the period in question.

Researchers have proposed a verification process for quantum computation that could withstand the potential failure of quantum computers to follow the correct physics. However, this process has a significant flaw: it is excessively slow, needing resources proportional to the number of quantum operations. We have devised an innovative approach that substantially improves the verification process, making it possible to do so in linear time, an advancement that has eluded experts for over two decades. We have successfully applied this method to both the quantum Turing machine and the quantum circuit models, and our results indicate that the underlying problem is not only solvable in polynomial time but also has a simple and efficient solution that involves verifying the quantum computation's output by comparing it to the classical computation's output, using the quantum computer's state via a measure-once measurement, and integrating the results of any multiple output measurements into a single output. We have further discovered that the key to our success involves a previously overlooked aspect of quantum computers: the ability to store and retrieve useful information even after the computation is complete.

Recent breakthroughs in neural radiance fields have greatly advanced the creation of implicit 3D objects with variable shapes. Researchers have successfully used these models to create numerous objects such as humans, animals, and inanimate items. However, these models have yet to be effectively applied to the creative modeling of living cell forms, which often exhibit complex and irregular shapes. In this research, we explore the cell morphology's implicit representation using neural radiance fields and find that existing techniques struggle to accurately model cells due to their irregular shapes and the lack of sufficient training data. To overcome these challenges, we introduce a novel implicit shape function, guided by a linear field that accommodates irregular shapes, and establish a new low-dimensional latent space that facilitates easy modeling and manipulation of cells. We evaluate our approach by comparing it to conventional methods, and demonstrate its efficacy through the creation of novel cell shapes, as well as the synthesis of missing data during training.

Reinforcement learning offers valuable insights into how agents interact with their environment. Successful training requires suitable geographic and meteorological conditions in the game world (simulator). Researchers found that certain training methods, such as using global maps with randomly assigned weather and terrain, often fail to produce effective agents. In contrast, training on tailored environments with optimized conditions leads to better performance. A key challenge lies in developing a suitable geographic representation that facilitates learning. While inspired by biological processes such as embryonic development, geographic representation lacks a clear biological foundation, making its choice crucial for training. By examining reinforcement learning outcomes in various environments, researchers gained insights into the complexities of geographic representation and learned to control environmental conditions for optimal training results.

In the study of stochastic systems, a specific type of non-reversible Markov chain setup is being explored, where certain transitions are inherently one-way. It's been discovered that the likelihood of a system transitioning from state A to state B is not the same as from state B to state A. Building on this, a more general framework, referred to as a $\mathcal{R}$-Markov chain, is established to capture this asymmetry, with the particular case of a reversible system being dubbed $\mathcal{0}$-Markov chain. The concept of system reversibility is related to the parity of the system's transition matrix and the set of allowable states, with these properties sufficient to determine the system's reversible nature. A specific $\mathcal{R}$-Markov chain model, the hard-drive dipoles system, is created using a place-dependent model inspired by ferromagnetic materials, where each site's state depends on its proximity to magnetic dipoles and the system's overall symmetry constraints. This model serves as a theoretical representation of systems with inherent asymmetry, with the system's irreversibility being ensured by the limited accessibility of certain state configurations.

The challenge of localizing multiple sound sources has been tackled in this research by proposing an innovative network design, incorporating Sound Position Estimation with Channel Rotation and Rectangular Filters (SPERCRRF), a Convolutional Recurrent Neural Network. This method uses sound wave samples as input, transforming them into spatial filters via an Angular Position Estimation module, then fine-tunes these filters to optimize detection of nearby sound sources. A Loss Minimization module in a Recurrent Neural layer sequentializes the data, enabling multi-source localization. Channel augmentation and rectangular filter modification, served as data pre-processing techniques to enhance the system's accuracy. A practical evaluation was conducted using a dataset comprising recordings from a microphone array in a car. Results demonstrated that SPERCRRF surpassed the performance of a conventional Convolutional Recurrent Neural Network, achieving more precise localization and better classification of sound sources.

Concurrent transmission based wireless systems hold promise for enhanced data rates and efficiency in emerging applications. This article surveys recent advancements in superposition transmission based systems, including non-linear coding techniques, convex optimization methods, and resource allocation strategies. These advancements have been successfully applied in areas such as unlicensed spectrum use, device-to-device communications, and machine-to-machine networks, leading to improved performance. While the article focuses on superposition transmission, it acknowledges the existence of other concurrent transmission methods, revealing their distinct advantages.

The inherent structure of a spectrogram is analyzed using stochastic geometry techniques to develop a framework for signal examination. A geometric process is created to represent spectrogram level contours, enabling the derivation of critical parameters, such as the density of extrema and the distribution of local energy, which are crucial for characterizing a spectrogram's topology. These parameters serve as markers for detecting signals and estimating their properties. A density indicator of extrema is proposed as a novel feature for distinguishing signals and background noise. Similarly, an ratio of local energies is proposed as a distinctive feature with the potential to characterize a spectrogram's tonal structure.

In complex network systems comprising interconnected spiking neurons, chimeras and synchronized groups persist even after significant disturbances. This phenomenon has significant implications in both neural and bio-medical contexts, given the widespread occurrence of chimeras in these fields. However, detecting chimeras and synchronized groups in large networks poses a major challenge due to their inherent state dependence. In response to this issue, a novel and robust method grounded in localized current injection has been developed. By analyzing the induced spike patterns in two distinct regimes, this strategy can unambiguously identify chimeras and synchronized groups at a minimal cost. Furthermore, our technique remains insensitive to errors in spike detection and is adaptable to networks with varied neuron types. In line with this goal, our method has been thoroughly validated through its successful application to multiple exemplary use cases.

The module rffree, randomly generating forces in the REBOUND N-body code, is introduced. It offers a tool to visualize and analyze random disturbances with various gauges, including the Newtonian and relativistic frameworks. With rffree, users can study the impact of random forces on N-body systems and explore how these disturbances affect their evolution. The tool is particularly useful for investigating the stability and life expectancy of planetary orbits. Furthermore, rffree provides a means to test the reliability of synthetic arguments made in celestial mechanics. With this module, REBOUND's capabilities are enhanced to explore the probability of interloper planets arising from random perturbations of a hypothetical terrestrial planet located in a zone affected by a giant planet.

We've developed a comprehensive approach using the quantum Fokker-Planck equation to design continuous feedback control systems that maintain stability around an optimal state. Our method employs two key methods: first, we leverage the quantum master equation to derive a relevant operator; next, we utilize the quantum Fokker-Planck equation to calculate the desired probability distribution of the controlled system. By combining these methods, we formulate a continuous feedback control system that achieves two crucial goals - maintaining stability and minimizing disruption - with our approach outlined in a publicly available GitHub repository.

We explore two-dimensional packed disks of varying sizes, trapped between a wall and an channel, especially focusing on how particle packing density and width of the channel are interconnected. Our research reveals a series of periodic states, each consisting of a specific pattern of larger and smaller particles, alternating in size. These particles alternate in a pattern that relates to Fibonacci sequence. Our analysis shows that these periodic states transition into a complex, non-repeating pattern as the particle sizes converge. We've observed similar patterns in three-dimensional packed spheres, trapped between walls of unequal widths. These patterns indicate that these configurations typically exhibit less packed density than perfectly packed structures. Moreover, our research was able to make connections between unique geometric arrangements and unique sets of particle sizes.

Research into different types of El Ni\~no-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) has indicated that each variant exhibits distinct precipitation responses in various parts of the world. In this study, we examine how various ENSO types affect global precipitation patterns, with a particular focus on regions experiencing both heavy and light precipitation. Using multiple ENSO types such as Central Pacific AC-type, Eastern Pacific EP-type, EP(el-Ni\~no) and CP(cp-Ni\~no), we analyze the responses in selected regions and compare them to the responses triggered by the two dominant ENSO phenomena, La Ni\~na and El Ni\~no. Our findings are based on a long-term simulation using the Precipitation Recycling Model, which has been proven to effectively capture various ENSO-related precipitation patterns in the Amazon and tropical Africa. Our results reveal that each ENSO type produces distinctive precipitation patterns in over 1,500 globally monitored sites. To evaluate the statistical significance of these patterns, we use a reliable bootstrap test. Our analysis further explores the relationships between the phases of ENSO and unusual precipitation events, confirming that certain ENSO phenomena are more frequently associated with such events. Our work has potential applications in improving the prediction and management of rare and extreme precipitation events worldwide.

A long-standing mystery in the field of massive black holes persists. It involves understanding the extensive range of massive black hole masses found at the centers of various types of galaxies, including both large and small ones. This problem has been divided into two components by researchers. First, they need to explain how the seeds of these massive black holes originated and second, they need to understand the processes by which the seeds developed into the massive black holes we see today. This research focuses on the second challenge and proposes a new hypothesis. It suggests that even small galaxies can host massive black hole ancestors and tests this idea using the low massive black hole density in small galaxies. A specific example is the low massive black hole density in the galaxy Leo I. This hypothesis is supported by the discovery of a dense stellar cluster in the galaxy Leo I hosting its black hole ancestor. Additionally, researchers have calculated the probability of discovering such a system in the nearby region and found it to be quite high. Finally, this research demonstrates that even though the known systems supporting massive black hole ancestors do not fit the typical large black hole development pathway, they can still provide valuable insights into understanding how the massive black holes we see today developed.

In materials with flat bands, which have an exceptional electronic property, unique behaviors can appear that diverge from typical band structures. We have discovered flat band induced adverse magnetoresistance in the classical multi-orbital Kagome metal, FeSn. When FeSn transitions from a non-magnetic state to a magnetized state, an unusual decrease in electrical resistance is observed, despite the typical increase seen in most magnets. The occurrence of flat bands in this process is confirmed through computational analysis, and the response can be optimized using magnetic field strength and orientation. The unusual properties of flat bands in Kereen materials may lead to the natural creation of quantum loops and other complex patterns, and our research serves as a starting point for exploring these phenomena.

The goal of this study is to provide a comprehensive examination of the shared genetic influences underlying complex human traits and behaviors. By combining the findings of genome-wide association studies, we sought to identify areas of the genome with significant associations and explore the functional characteristics of these regions using data from various public and proprietary sources. Through a collaborative effort, we examined 18 distinct traits and behaviors, uncovering novel insights into their underlying genomic mechanisms. Notably, our analysis revealed a substantial presence of functional elements within regions associated with complex traits, underscoring the importance of accurately annotating genomic information to accurately interpret the results of genome-wide association studies.

Consider a group of symmetries acting on a set of objects, where this action is reduced to a lower-level representation when we focus on a specific subset of the objects' arrangements. This scenario occurs when a group of symmetries is transitive on both the objects and their arrangements. A particular category of these group actions encompasses situations where the subgroup of symmetries that preserve object structure has no non-trivial inactions on individual objects, implying each object remains unchanged under such preservation. A distinct type of group action within this category is characterized by no non-trivial inactions on the objects as a whole, resulting in no inactions on their arrangements either. A specific instance of this category consists of actions with no inactions on the objects as a whole, yielding direct transitivity on their arrangements. A different instance is marked by a single arrangement being invariant under the group action, leading to transitive action on the resulting arranged components. This study focuses on a particular sub-instance where this invariance leads to non-transitive action on the arranged components and investigates the resulting arranged components' commutants, which represent the sub-groups of symmetries that remain unchanged under the group action. Using recent combinatorial classification of actions with transitive arrangement properties, we identify all instances where this invariance occurs and examine the resulting arranged components' commutants in detail, revealing their isomorphism to sub-groups of symmetries acting on a specific arrangement structure.

The behavior of entropes derived from a zero-range model of Coulomb interaction for two-electron atoms is examined, particularly focusing on carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen as these elements were initially used by Pauling to estimate the number of electrons in atoms based on bond length data. We compute interaction energies for these atoms in their ground states, employing entropes formulated by Hirschfelder, in which electron spins are treated as distinct entities. The results show that for all atoms under consideration, the entropes used by Pauling to estimate interaction energies are too low, resulting in underestimations of 10%, 20%, and 30% for nitrogen, carbon, and oxygen, respectively. Nonetheless, for nitrogen, the entropes with and without spin considerations differ by no more than 35 keV. We propose that the Hirschfelder entropes, both with and without accounting for spin, be used as reference points for estimating bond length data associated with atoms such as hydrogen, lithium, boron, fluorine, sodium, phosphorus, chlorine, potassium, arsenic, strontium, and scandium.

The operation of a clock is influenced by a particle's gravitational activity, both internally and externally, according to certain theories. Past research has examined how external gravity affects a particle, revealing that its impact varies proportionally with the gravitational field's strength, or equivalently, its gravitational potential. Conversely, a particle's internal gravitational activity, or extensive binary test, is believed to be unaffected by external gravity. Historically, the tests conducted so far have been based on simple, harmonic oscillators. This study seeks to expand upon this by utilizing a quadratic oscillator, a more complex model with a restored force counteracting dispersion, commonly observed in nature. Our findings indicate that the internal gravitational activity of a quadratic oscillator remains unaltered in the presence of external gravity, mirroring the results obtained from harmonic oscillators.

In the course of proving the soundness and completeness of a structural proof theory for multiplicative linear logic with an excluded middle, a specific proof transformation is identified as equivalent to cut-elimination. This proof transformation can be seen as a structured version of cut-elimination, and it offers an alternative to the standard proof transformation used in structural proof theory.

Predictive analysis in financial time series is complex due to their inherently unpredictable nature, making it challenging to identify indicators of approaching synchronization within these series. This study employs cross-recurrence diagrams and quantifies synchronization in stock market time series, including Google's share price and the UK's FTSE, comparing different trading environments to determine how global events affect market correlation.

Thermal influences on particles in transport systems have been extensively explored in terms of their inherent inertia. However, when it comes to electron-phonon and spin-vibration interactions, the impact of phonon and spin Inertia remains poorly understood. This research employs a formalism grounded in a thermal Hamiltonian to reveal that both electron-phonon and spin-vibration interactions are subject to significant dynamic influences stemming from phonon and spin inertia, resulting in multiple virtual processes. A computational model will be used to illustrate how these processes affect the electronic and spin transport properties across nanostructures. This study addresses a critical knowledge gap and paves the way for a new class of thermoelectric materials.

Current click-through rate (CTR) forecasting systems are primarily dependent on historical user behavior, which may lead to inaccuracies when predicting CTR for fresh ads lacking contextual information. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a novel CTR forecasting framework that incorporates ad visual content to improve forecasting precision. By extracting essential information from each advertisement, our system generates highly accurate click predictions, ultimately resulting in enhanced revenue maximization for online advertising platforms. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that our approach outperforms the standard CTR forecasting model, with improved mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) and eightfold increased revenue.

Business process management systems rely on case management to address irregular processes. Existing approaches for modeling business processes with specific characteristics often overlook the relationships between processes. This can lead to invalid process models that are difficult to understand, causing issues such as process execution and analysis problems. This paper addresses the challenges of process awareness and inheritance in business processes by developing a framework for constraining the size of process subsets. It includes methods for detecting constraints, calculating the minimum required constraints, and addressing the problem of finding the best constraints. This paper also presents a method for identifying the most relevant constraints, based on the concepts of impact and reachability. An evaluation using real-world data showed that this approach is efficient and confirmed its technical innovations.

Quantifying wildfires' impact on a global scale is essential for assessing their health effects on people. However, accurately tracking wildfires is often hindered by the sparsity and irregularity of satellite imagery data, particularly spatial and temporal disparities. To address this, we've developed an innovative approach using an integrated system of informed statistical models, tailored to utilize diverse satellite images, such as MODIS, VIIRS, and GOES-16. By employing a physics-based framework to bridge the gap between measurements and simulations, our model achieves precise representation and forecasting of wildfire aerosols. Notably, our approach successfully incorporates the inherent noises and variations inherent in noisy remote sensing data, resulting in improved density estimation and forecasting capabilities. This has significant implications for accurately modeling wildfires, a crucial step in estimating aerosols levels. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method through comprehensive simulations and real-world applications, outperforming competing methods in forecasting precision and model complexity.

Recent research has focused on evaluating the privacy risks associated with selecting specific locations from hypothetical prior distributions, with a particular focus on Gaussian Conditional Priors. This paper seeks to address two unaddressed aspects of this problem - how to measure privacy and determine when an image can be reconstructed from a given location. Our findings indicate that the Fourier Transform is not a sufficient tool for assessing this particular type of privacy and that we can derive more accurate conclusions regarding the reconstruction of locations with specific characteristics. Additionally, we investigate how to generalize the results obtained for 1D to their 2D analogs.

Research has shown that estimating functional connectivity using multisite fMRI data typically yields less precise results compared to single-site data, likely due to decreased data availability and inter-site connectivity variability. To better understand this phenomenon, we conducted a comprehensive statistical analysis of multisite data and observed that lower precision comes at the cost of reduced confidence in estimated connections. To address this issue, we developed two strategies: (1) developing site-specific models to minimize inter-site connectivity variability; (2) employing Bayesian shrinkage estimation to aggregate information across sites and increase precision. Our research demonstrates that these approaches effectively improve prediction accuracy when comparing single-site and multisite data. To facilitate widespread adoption, we have made our code publicly available on GitHub.

Building on the concept of Concentration of Measure introduced by Bolthausen and Garnett-Ganghi in 2019, we make two significant contributions. Firstly, we establish a new inequality for directed network maps, which leads to a relevant lower bound on the directed Ricci curvature. Secondly, we demonstrate a phenomenon called Concentration of Measure, where a particular function's disparity in values across different points in a directed network diminishes exponentially, and the rate of this concentration is directly proportional to the square of the distance between these points, under a condition of positive Ricci curvature. Furthermore, we investigate the rate of concentration for directed networks with lower bounded Ricci curvature, and find that it surpasses the exponent obtained in a previous study by Cesa-Bielli et al in 2020, which was relevant to undirected networks.

Recent advances in NLP have led to significant interest in code-mixed social media texts. These texts, used extensively in the Indian region, blend multiple languages, posing a challenge to process them effectively. Current approaches rely on pre-defined vocabulary lists that fail to capture the dynamic nature of code-mixed languages with evolving words and languages. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a new encoder, known as Transition-based Positional Encoding Transition Point (TP-PE), capable of identifying language shifts within these texts. We also develop a novel embedding technique, called Relative position encoding for code-mixed languages, and combine it with a Transformer model for better performance. We evaluate our approach on top of two relevant tasks: language identification and Bilingual named entity recognition, and observe improved results on publicly available datasets. Notably, our TP-PE outperforms established methods, including established positional encoding techniques, on these tasks.

Using a quasi-one-dimensional molecular chain model with intermolecular interactions, we calculate the phonon spectra of H$_{3}$S under various pressures. The model allows for a quasi-one-dimensional motion along the c-axis and a two-dimensional motion within the ab-plane, which results in a complex dispersion curve with a Van Hove singularity at the zone edge. Consistently, our simulations using the Jahn-Teller effective mass approach for electron-phonon interactions reveal a significant impact on the phonon spectrum, particularly on the 6th phonon branch. Applying the Lawrence-Doniach model for s-wave superconductivity, we find that both the superconducting gap ratio and critical temperature are highly dependent on the 6th phonon branch and are increased under pressure, with T$_{c}$ reaching its maximum at 203 K for a 230 GPa pressure. However, when considering isotopic mixing with a 50% S and 50% N composition, our results show a substantial decrease in the superconducting gap ratio and a significant drop in T$_{c}$ down to 64 K, which is attributed to the broadening of the phonon spectrum and reduced Van Hove singularity.

Fisher's fundamental theorem in evolutionary biology seeks to link the rate of morphological change to the rate of genetic change, with the latter being measured by the covariance between a trait and genetic variables. However, there has been significant debate over the correctness of Fisher's theorem, particularly regarding its derivation and scope. A common issue in addressing this controversy has been the confusion of causal and correlational relationships. A key challenge in understanding Fisher's theorem is determining a valid representation of causal effects in terms of the model's parameters. A critical concept in addressing this problem is the notion of a "mean effect," which designates the expected value of a particular causal parameter. A key finding of this study is that the mean effect can be utilized as a precise pointer, effectively dismissing any derivations not aligning with it. A central assertion of this study is that the mean effect can take on the form of a linear combination of variables' effects, including those of the trait and genetic variables. A significant implication of this finding is that the mean effect can exhibit directionality despite its non-causality, highlighting the importance of distinguishing between the mean effect and the rate of morphological change.

This paper proposes an innovative technique for bipedal locomotion that incorporates propellant-assisted steps. By utilizing leg movements similar to those used in the rocket jump technique, animals can achieve significant vertical jumps. However, the proposed strategy goes beyond simple impulse transfers, incorporating complex optimizations that enable efficient energy usage and stable tailoring of the push-off force for successful takeoff. Mathematical modeling of a humanoid robot's dynamics was conducted to develop a quantitative analysis of the proposed movement pattern. Computer simulations confirmed the potential benefits of this method in producing propellant-enhanced steps. Furthermore, the research demonstrated that the new strategy can produce similar movement outcomes to traditional bipedalism while reducing the magnitude of foot forces or increasing walking speeds with comparable stability levels. Additionally, it was observed that specific movement patterns can reduce robot balance challenges.

Achieving visual relocalization in partially observable environments relies on precise geometric and photometric alignment. Despite effective pre-training methods, downstream tasks struggle with achieving high relocalization accuracy in unfamiliar environments. This research presents a two-stage visual relocalization approach combining pre-trained surfel maps, employing planar geometric primitives to establish a common framework between maps and scenes. A unique two-step learning procedure is used to derive key visual features from images, matching pre-trained maps using these derived features. The outcome is a robust relocalization method with minimal dependence on visible keypoints in images, enabling accurate placement of a camera within a pre-built surfel map. Experimental results using the TUM dataset show our method surpasses state-of-the-art monocular relocalization techniques, with a successful relocalization rate of 93.5% in unknown environments.

Mobile devices can learn from labeled data, but model accuracy suffers from model communication inefficiencies and data ambiguity caused by client device variability. This research optimizes a new technique that combines the benefits of customized federated semi-supervised learning and efficient model communication. A proposed ambiguity reduction method uses two layers of neural networks to identify and clarify ambiguous data classes on the edge, then aligns local classes with a global class structure using a federated clustering algorithm. This method reduces data ambiguity and improves model communication efficiency. Experimental results show that our method achieves higher accuracy and faster convergence than related studies.

Simulations of colliding a black hole with a neutron star have been conducted in a series of general-relativistic numerical simulations. These collisions are studied from different perspectives, including various initial magnetic field configurations and equations of state for the neutron star. Typically, these events result in a massive, rapidly spinning disk forming around the black hole due to the disruption of the neutron star. Additionally, a massive, low-density cloud of disk material is driven away from the center of the collision in a phenomenon known as a "neutron star cloud'. Several key factors, such as the neutron star cloud's mass and angular velocity, as well as its final location and shape, are significantly influenced by equations of state and magnetic fields in these simulations. Notably, more rigid equations of state and stronger magnetic fields tend to result in more massive neutron star clouds. In contrast, softer equations of state and weaker magnetic fields lead to a greater amount of disk material being formed. A notable exception occurs when considering neutron star clouds in collisions with very weak magnetic fields, in which case even softer equations of state still result in smaller neutron star clouds due to the influence of magnetic fields.

A distorted metric on a closed Riemann surface can be degenerate except for possibly one point, and a specific distortion degree exists regardless of whether the metric is degenerate or not. The distortion degree relates to the volume of the metric region containing a chosen disk and a chosen metric on that region that is comparable to the original metric. The distortion degree also has an alternative representation as the infimum of a specific integral involving a scalar curvature and weighted metrics. Furthermore, the distortion degree has applications in establishing various inequalities, such as a Poincare inequality, and a hard Sobolev inequality on closed Riemann surfaces.

This paper offers a straightforward demonstration of the fact that a sequence of conditioned processes converging to a given process also converges to the process conditioned on never exiting a specified domain. Our proof employs a relatively simple approach compared to the method in Stepenson (2018) and addresses a notable omission in the argument presented in Stephens (2017), proving that a sequence of Markov processes converging to a target process also converges to the target process conditioned on never exiting a specified domain. Our work includes a few additional results, including a statement regarding the long-term stability of certain self-transition rates and the demonstration of convergence of the Q-process to the target process for a broad class of non-irreducible Markov processes.

The graphene surface plasmon resonance is a highly versatile tool due to its wide range of applications, including grapheme's unique optical properties. Although graphene's interaction with particles is primarily centered around its optical characteristics, the terahertz response of adhering nanoparticles suggests a previously underexplored mechanism. In our research, the attachment of nanoparticles to a graphene sheet is examined using numerical models, and the outcomes are supported by theoretical frameworks. The findings reveal that the interaction between the nanoparticles and graphene results in enhanced energy exchange and non-radiative coupling, causing the nanoparticles to adhere. The analysis indicates that this effect is driven by the irregularities in the graphene's electric structure, rather than the dipole interaction commonly observed. The research demonstrates that graphene's surface plasmons can operate effectively at terahertz frequencies, and the fixed energy exchange between the graphene and nanoparticles achieves remarkable adhesion strength. The findings have significant implications for graphene's use in chemical sensing, biological recognition, and other nanoparticle-based technologies.

In the urgent environment of an emergency setting, deciding how long an intervention should last can be a complex task. There's often limited understanding of how interventions evolve over time, making it challenging to determine the optimal duration. This study aimed to define typical intervention timelines in the emergency context and establish predictive models for each phase. Based on data from the Trauma Quality Improvement Project, the research identified and differentiated different patient groups, using unsupervised learning techniques. The results were then combined with clinical expertise to develop distinct patterns, defined by start and end times for each group. These patterns indicate the duration of interventions is highly variable, influenced by patients' conditions, and often unpredictable without prior knowledge. The study's findings offer a framework for guiding intervention lengths in the emergency field, with potential applications in developing more realistic simulation scenarios and training systems.

A novel approach to long-term autonomous cooperation is proposed for a group of robots with limited computational capacity, operating within a challenging environmental setup characterized by predictable dynamics and bounded disturbances. Each robot utilizes a basic decision-making strategy rooted in one-step look-ahead planning, focusing on executing previously planned actions despite potential disruptions. It is demonstrated that the overall stability of the system can be ensured through a specific network structure among the robots and a control strategy, even in the presence of excessive information exchange. This information exchange is optimized to minimize the robots' performance loss, taking into account the robots' initial conditions and a measure of cooperation. Furthermore, it is shown that the stability of the system can also be maintained with reduced and variable information exchange, restricted to local exchanges among robots with better awareness of their surroundings. This awareness is measured by a metric of relative statefulness.

Data from Pb-Pb collisions at 2.76 and 5.02 TeV were analyzed to study particle distributions in terms of centrality, azimuthal separation, and charge dependence. This analysis aimed to quantify correlations between charges in collisions that may be influenced by the Chiral Magnetic Effect (CME). By examining correlations in both same- and opposite-charge pairs, and considering events with charges of at least three, our study found that these distributions can be accurately represented by a model that incorporates correlations caused by the fragmentation of charged particles. Furthermore, our research revealed that correlations potentially influenced by CME effects are largely negligible in events with charges exceeding three. Within this study, we also present initial observations of CME-like influences in collisions that may be related to the interaction of CME and charged-particle interactions.

The surge in crowd-sourced funding research has sparked a high demand for a comprehensive understanding of the key factors contributing to successful online fundraising campaigns. Although numerous studies have conducted exploratory analysis on crowd behaviors, there is a significant need for a unified framework that can effectively identify and compare these behaviors across different platforms. This research aims to establish a unified framework by examining and validating a set of established metrics across three prominent platforms, including Kickstarter, Indiegogo, and FundedNext. By analyzing the performance of these metrics using regression models, we have found that a combination of crowd engagement and online fundraising campaign management play a crucial role in determining a campaign's success. Furthermore, our analysis suggests that the absolute funding goal of a campaign can positively affect its success, whereas the campaign's popularity and duration have a contrasting impact. To address the issue of pseudo-negative campaigns, we have proposed a novel metric called the Success Rate metric and observed that it can effectively identify such cases. This research has several platform-specific findings, highlighting the unique characteristics of each platform. Notably, the results have shown that the performance of the metrics can vary significantly across platforms, emphasizing the need for further research on the fundamental differences among crowdfunding platforms.

As cyber threats evolve, businesses face increased pressure to monitor their systems, requiring the exchange of sensitive information to stay ahead. Nevertheless, the sharing of cyber intelligence is hindered by concerns regarding data confidentiality. A potential solution has been proposed in this research, utilizing a novel combination of federated learning and watermarking techniques to address the challenges of information exchange and data ownership verification. A proposed cyber threat intelligence sharing framework integrates these concepts, featuring an intelligent detection model based on combined deep learning and physics-based simulations. This approach is evaluated using real-world data from Intrusion Detection Scenario B, and the results indicate a 94% success rate in verifying ownership and 97% in exchanging relevant intelligence. Furthermore, the study highlights a 34% improvement in classification accuracy compared to standard intrusion detection methods.

The area of service robotics, encompassing domains such as logistics and healthcare, is characterized by complex robotic mission sequences that involve enhanced efficiency through clustering-oriented strategies in European Conference on Artificial Intelligence Conference Proceedings, Volume 19 (2004), pages 748-753, addresses the crucial problem of minimizing total robotic manipulation time by combining multiple tasks efficiently. Unlike previous research, which confined optimization to individual tasks, the paper introduces a more comprehensive approach that considers the sequential deployment of robots to multiple locations. To achieve this, the authors developed an effective greedy algorithm capable of delivering near-optimal outcomes, particularly for large-scale robotic missions. Unlike other methods, the proposed solution avoids excessive computational expenses, making it highly suitable for real-time application in service robotics.

The trend towards more aggressive technology nodes necessitates a substantial increase in device complexity, causing a significant rise in development costs. Considering the limitations associated with advanced nodes, a possible solution involves leveraging existing, established CMOS processes to manufacture Silicon-MOSFETs. However, achieving high performance would require the introduction of novel materials or novel channel materials. One feasible option is the use of MoS2 for the semiconductor material to form a 2D FET. Similarly, Se-based materials or other chalcogenide materials could be used. In our research, we manufactured 2D FETs using a 300mm CMOS process employing a Si substrate with a lateral gauge of 20nm. The demonstrated devices exhibit substantial mobility (>2000 cm2/Vs) and high switching speed (>100ns), showcasing the potential of silicon-based technologies to overcome supply shortages of critical materials and achieve significant performance milestones.

In any team setting, optimal performance is heavily dependent on a balanced combination of intragroup skills and relationships. This study employs a special type of neural network, with each member having unique abilities and/or access to exclusive information, that works together to navigate dynamic environments. Our main objectives are to 1) understand how different member abilities affect team performance, 2) identify strategies for handling discrepancies in how team members process information, and 3) learn how team members' interactions impact their coordination. Our findings suggest that such interactions indeed play a crucial role in how well a team performs and that each team member's contribution, as well as how they work together, significantly affects their overall performance.

A significant challenge in ensuring video search engines are fair involves assessing their performance on diverse groups. Most existing tests rely on predetermined attributes such as age and gender, but they fail to account for more complex personality differences such as cultural background and personal interests. To overcome these limitations, we developed a new virtual agent-based system that can measure bias in search outcomes by collecting extensive data on user interactions in a virtual environment. Our study demonstrates the effectiveness of this method by auditing a major video platform and revealing a bias towards origins preferred by a majority of users, but also uncovering a subtle preference for a particular origin that doesn't reflect the preferences of our virtual users.

To address challenges in quantum gravity and Algebrisca, researchers are exploring the consistency of quantum theories, particularly those with defected monodromy properties. A key challenge lies in the absence of reliable bootstrapping methods for such theories when compared to their well-defined, linear counterparts. We developed an innovative nonlinear bootstrapping approach, applicable to theories lacking interactions, and successfully applied it to a non-linear extension of the Wess-Zumino model. This extension features a unique charge-3 operator, which diverges from its linear counterpart. We discovered that by imposing specific constraints on the spectral density, the conformal block expansion becomes analytically computable. Furthermore, our findings reveal that the non-interacting Wess-Zumino model adheres to string theory, fitting within the AdS$_3$/CFT$_2$ framework. This result, validated through global matching, confirms that the model's conformal data is uniquely determined by the spectral density at the three-point level.

We find 17 elliptic curves defined over cyclic cubic fields, such as cubic fields derived from factorizations of $j$-invariants, with a point on each curve increasing its rank by one, using four different methods. A 2015 computation by Kwon and Lee initially discovered 11 curves. We discover an additional six curves for this purpose. These curves together provide over 40% of all elliptic curves defined over these fields with ranks 13 or higher. We also find that elliptic curves with ranks 13 or higher are concentrated in certain subfields of $\Q(\zeta_3)$.

In densely deployed Wireless Local Area Networks, utilizing the 2.4 GHz ISM band can be problematic due to interference from other WLANs. However, by wisely managing local traffic, a new strategy aims to mitigate interference from other WLANs, addressing a long-standing blind spot in existing QoS frameworks. Existing studies primarily focus on countering interference from other WLANs, but this new approach targets minimizing local traffic's detrimental impact. It leverages a non-parametric, non-parametric stochastic medium access control (WSMAC) framework to optimize local traffic generation based on real-time local traffic and interference statistics. By applying a high-dimensional Markov model, the system optimizer solves a complex optimization problem, and a near-optimal, high-dimensional coding strategy is developed. Further, the theoretical findings are confirmed through simulations, demonstrating that the WSMA framework outperforms the traditional time division multiple access (TDMA) and current best best effort scheduling methods.

Graph Neural Networks have demonstrated remarkable performance in graph classification. However, a major challenge lies in scaling label propagation on large graphs. A significant problem arises when some nodes on these graphs require manual labeling due to limited access points. To address these issues, we devise a novel approach that integrates pseudo-labeling and node sampling techniques. Our method utilizes two neural networks: one to generate high-quality pseudo-labels for invisible nodes and another to select influential nodes with accurate labels. Through extensive experiments on diverse graph classification benchmarks, we demonstrate the efficacy of our approach and showcase its superiority over existing benchmark methods. Notably, our approach achieves impressive generalization performance on large graphs and outperforms traditional pseudo-labeling methods when labels are readily available. You can access the code for this paper at https://github.com/AIE8090/PL-GNN.

In our research, we introduce PatchNet, a novel framework for performing short-range video alignment efficiently. Traditional large-scale alignment methods are hindered by lengthy synchronization processes. We devise PatchNet to tackle this challenge by accelerating the alignment of individual frames and facilitating temporal propagation to achieve optimal results. Leveraging a straightforward yet effective design, PatchNet yields speedy processing of frames, with a minimal latency of one frame, for large-scale video alignment. Furthermore, it maintains accuracy by incorporating temporal information, thereby outperforming current leading methods even when using a single GPU. Notably, PatchNet achieves a significant boost of up to 3x in processing speed, with a minimal increase of only 1x in memory requirements.

We examine a one-dimensional, multi-species version of the TASEP with time periodic rates in a finite system. The rates for each species are predetermined and follow specific patterns. The expected behavior of TASEP is to reach a state of detailed balance. However, since the rates are subject to periodic fluctuations, we can anticipate a time-periodic arrangement of particles. The problem of distributing particles at a specific time period is equivalent to an integer partitioning problem, in which we divide a certain number of items into equal parts. The total number of possible partitions can grow factorially as the system scales, which presents a significant computational challenge. By gathering data on the number of possible partitions for smaller systems, we can gather insights on how these arrangements behave in larger systems.

A novel approach, known as SWIPT, enables simultaneous data transfer and energy transfer to devices within a single network transaction. However, optimizing energy harvesting rates also depends on achieving an equilibrium between power splitting (PS) ratios and achieving sufficient decoding quality for both communication devices. To address this, we introduce a resource allocation scheme, combining PS and power allocation, designed for multi-service networks. Each device utilizes a general-purpose processor, enabled to run various applications. A detailed system model is developed, focusing on a processor's capability to run multiple applications, along with a power allocation strategy for maximizing energy transfer while ensuring an acceptable communication quality. To prevent interference between applications and data transfer, we utilize a matrix inversion approach. A circulant matrix can efficiently facilitate large-scale power allocation, including energy transfer. Despite the nonconvex nature of the resulting problem, we present a simplified approach, reducing the circulant matrix inversion and present alternative solutions. Comprehensive simulations validate the efficiency and effectiveness of the proposed approach.

The SU(N) Fermi gases with negative interactions serve as an optimal framework to explore novel phenomena resulting from both high excitation energies and strong interactions in ultra-cold gases, going beyond the realm of traditional Fermi liquids. In this context, we provide an in-depth analysis of the properties of the interaction matrix for the SU(N) Fermi gases with a focus on the 1/3 degenerate interaction in the SU(3) Fermi gases, revealing its distinct general structure from other repulsive interactions like the U(1) Fermi gases. Our findings show that this new interaction gives rise to a unique generalized version of the Fermi liquid behavior, yielding precise closed-form expressions of the energy spectrum, low-energy excitation energy, specific heat, magnetic moment, spin susceptibility, and particle correlation function. Furthermore, we establish a new theoretical framework to study the properties of the bound state in the SU(3) Fermi gases with a 1/3 degenerate interaction in deep attractive regime, predicting its binding energy, energy shift, and particle correlation function. Our theoretical framework is validated by comparison with the available QMC simulation data, and the results indicate that it is possible to extend our new theoretical framework to the SU(N) Fermi gases with a 1/(N+1) degenerate interaction.

We present a simple electrical circuit model that mimics specific aspects of microwave optomechanics. This model is based on the classical mechanics of a particular type of optomechanical system and employs circuit elements commonly used in analytical and numerical studies of electrical circuits. Our main goal is to demonstrate that the optomechanical system's behavior, characterized by a mixture of electrical and mechanical interactions, can be effectively represented by the circuit model. This is achieved by modeling the optomechanical system's eigenmodes as standing waves, with the resulting eigenfrequencies and quality factors equivalent to those of the circuit model. Furthermore, we show that the optomechanical system's eigenstates, described in terms of quantized radiation and phonon states, correspond to resonant responses in the circuit model, with relationships defined by impedance spectroscopy.

Witten's $Q$-box graph theory originates from two distinct sources - airship structure and matrix perturbation - which are connected to the focus on non-interacting fermions in specific geometric constraints. The $Q$-box graph is defined by an underlying undirected graph, where the $Q$-form simplifies to an Airy function polynomial on graphs that are trees. The concept of Witten's $Q$-box graph theory extends to a broader set of finite graphs, where we demonstrate that the $Q$-form can be expressed as a universal Airy polynomial applicable to all graphs, revealing its underlying symmetry and allowing for a simplified, yet general, representation. The proposed Witten's $Q$-box graph theory now encompasses a wide range of applications, from statistical mechanics and random matrix theory to quantum mechanics and information theory.

This research explores the problem of robots tracking a wall in a space with a grid-like pattern, which can shift unexpectedly. We've identified two types of grid patterns that cause robots to move erratically: one that changes in a predictable pattern (trend) and one that doesn't follow a pattern at all (stochastic). We've developed a model that shows how these trends can lead a robot to move erratically and even get stuck in certain situations. On the other hand, when the grid pattern is consistent and predictable (along a line or in a repeating pattern), we've found conditions that allow a robot to stay on track.

This article further explores and develops the concept of chiral aspects in 2dcft within the pAQFT framework, building upon a previously published study.  It specifically investigates how these aspects relate to a massless scalar field in globally hyperbolic 2-dimensional spacetimes.  The study identifies subalgebras that contain either chiral or anti-chiral observables, constructing these explicitly and showing they are embedded in the full theory's algebra.  It also establishes that the construction of these subalgebras is Cauchy surface-independent and yields a well-defined covariant theory on the space of null geodesics.

Smoke formation during laparoscopic surgery poses significant challenges, causing obstructed views and making it difficult for surgeons to assess the surgical environment. To address this issue, researchers have proposed using smoke detection through image processing of real-time video feed from laparoscopic cameras. However, smoke-laden images often appear dim and faded, making smoke detection increasingly difficult. To enhance smoke identification, researchers have explored the potential of smoke image improvement techniques. To determine if these image improvement methods are beneficial, we conducted a comprehensive study, comparing three enhancement techniques - Contrast Stretching, Histogram Equalization and Median Filter - for their effectiveness in enhancing smoke images, thereby improving automatic smoke detection. Our investigation involved two primary objectives: evaluating how image enhancement affects smoke detection accuracy and determining whether image enhancement can boost this accuracy. To mark non-smoke areas in our dataset, we employed a simple, previously established method, supplemented by additional information to generate ground truth labels for a more detailed analysis. To assess the impact of image enhancement on smoke detection, we employed various performance metrics, including precision, recall and F1-score. Our results indicate that image enhancement generally improves smoke detection accuracy, with Contrast Stretching and Histogram Equalization achieving higher precision, recall and F1-score values than a baseline approach. Notably, Histogram Equalization achieved the highest F1-score values across all models, with a significant improvement of 11.43% in precise smoke detection and 12.5% in recall. These findings suggest that image improvement can advantage

This research introduces a method to create stable molecular gates based on M{\o}lmer-S{\o}rensen interactions, utilizing multiple vibrational modes in an trap to achieve a robust performance. Through a straightforward cooling technique using a thermal bath, an equal superposition of motional states can be consistently reached, independent of frequency fluctuations between the laser and the trap. By combining this approach with a standard MS gate sequence, we demonstrate that it is possible to produce frequency-stable entanglement of up to hundreds of thousands of times per second, using a trap with a small number of photons. This innovative technique offers an efficient means to produce large amounts of entangled pairs for quantum networking and other applications.

Researchers employed a framework of "structural templates" to establish a microscopic image of paraelectric perovskites. A paraelectric perovskite, typically composed of a metal cation at its center, consists of a lattice of ions including A cations (large) and B cations (smaller), surrounded by oxygen ions. The existence of A cations at antinode positions significantly contributes to polarizations competing with the primary ion displacement, leading to increased stability of the paraelectric state. The arrangement of cations also affects the accessibility of the material, with certain metal cations restricting the transfer of electrons due to their placement within the lattice.

Decomposing a multivariate Gaussian distribution into lower-dimensional subgroups, as in Gaussian graphs, has significant applications in modeling and inference. While this concept is well-established for fixed-dimensional data, its extension to infinite dimensions, called functional Gaussian graphs, is less understood. This work builds upon the foundation of the functional Gaussian graph model introduced in a prior paper by coordinating and consolidating related concepts and demonstrating their equivalence to graphically defined Gaussian processes. We further explore the relationship between functional Gaussian graphs and Gaussian processes in this context.

Compiling a quantum circuit's instructions into executable units called instructions, or "gate sequences," shows varying performance depending on the used method. Some predictable algorithms, like Sequential Deep Shallow, demonstrate excellent compilation results for intricate circuits with repeating patterns in their instructions. We investigate why SDSh excels by analyzing its pattern detection abilities and the structure of learned sequences. Our analysis reveals that SDSh's compilation efficiency stems from its ability to recognize patterns in a circuit's instructions and generate optimized sequences that maximize gate sequence length. Notably, SDSh's optimized sequences exhibit lower energy, indicating lower costs, and are also less prone to errors and require less resource-intensive corrections.

A recent development in the study of machine learning models has led to the recognition of average-case learning, which surpasses traditional worst-case learning in insight and generality. In this context, we identify a specific type of average-case learning task and demonstrate that it encompasses a broad range of challenges, including those that require both strong computational assumptions and robust architectural designs. Specifically, we establish that average-case learning under uniform distribution involves learning convex functions on the unit hypercube. This line of inquiry is significant because it bridges the gap between symmetric and asymmetric learning problems, offering valuable insights into the fundamental characteristics of learning problems and their potential solutions.

We investigate a bilayer semiconductor system with indirect gaps, characterized by interlayer coupled wave functions, where which results in novel excitonic states across the layers. Strong coupling between photons and these unique excitons yields unique optical properties. Calculations indicate that these excitons form stable polaronic entities surrounded by a cloud of photons. The computational approach utilized is based on a self-consistent mean-field method.

Designing a reliable and self-adaptative sensor system for mobile devices that uses radio-based localization and tracking in indoor settings is a difficult task due to the problem of node outage. The probability of this occurring can be calculated using empirical methods, but they are not efficient in terms of computation. This paper presents a new method called adaptive probabilistic routing, which uses communication reliability data to create reliable paths for sending location data to a central node. The algorithm calculates the reliability of each link by taking into account the impact of packet loss and a variable time interval. Once a reliable path has been established, the algorithm determines the path with the highest probability of successful data transfer to the central node. The results of extensive simulations show that the algorithm outperforms existing methods, including those that use Markovian models and Monte Carlo simulations.

The standard model describes nature's fundamental particles and forces, with recently discovered W and Z bosons exhibiting two polarization states. However, experiments at the Large Hadron Collider have revealed that these bosons are jointly polarized when produced in certain interactions. A recent study involved analyzing $W^{\pm}Z$ pairs created through proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV. A statistically significant difference in charged boson polarization states was observed, consistent with the predicted relationship of 1:2. Additionally, measurements of boson polarization states have provided constraints on certain theories beyond the standard model, with constraints on a certain parameter, m_Z', having tightened to a range of -350 MeV to 300 MeV. A comparison with a theoretical model predicting an additional heavy boson showed that certain assumptions were inconsistent with experimental findings. A discovery or absence of joint polarization in $W^{\pm}Z$ pairs will offer crucial insights into nature at its most fundamental level.

The Cotton tensor is a well-defined gravitational field tensor that is widely used in two-dimensional gravity and as a divergence-free extension of the Einstein tensor in higher-dimensional gravity. However, the Cotton tensor's relationship to the gravitational field is not yet clearly understood in higher-dimensional gravity. This study aims to clarify this by establishing a theorem that relates the vanishing of the Cotton tensor to the global flatness of the gravitational field in higher dimensions, providing a more comprehensive understanding of two-dimensional gravity and setting a new standard for future research in higher-dimensional gravity.
A geometric duality applies to orthomodular lattices, establishing a one-to-one correspondence between geometries and lattices while preserving key properties.

The Coq Proof Diagram Visualiser is a visualisation tool that renders Coq proof scripts and other files into interactive diagrams, linking relevant elements together. Users can navigate these diagrams to explore dependencies between statements and proofs in facility-filled environments. The tool aims to facilitate comprehension, especially for those unfamiliar with proofs, by making diagrammatic representations of proof structures and content. It does this by treating proofs as graphs, where statements and proofs serve as nodes, and edges indicate included content. Users can import various Coq files, including proofs, libraries, and project structures, to generate visual representations of content within specified areas, or even the entire project. Additionally, the tool includes features for customising visual outputs, such as the ability to focus on a particular area, filter content, and highlight key elements. These visual representations can be saved as SVG files, enabling users to share and sharefully embed diagrammatic proofs and structures in other systems.

We demonstrate that the fourth moment of holomorphic Hecke cusp forms is limited under the assumption of the Riemann Hypothesis for a specific degree 8 L-function. This is achieved by leveraging the connection between these forms and a particular family of L-functions, as well as a complementary result derived from the noncentral fourth moment of a grid-based set of Dirichlet L-functions. This yields an accurate upper limit for the fourth moment of all Hecke cusp forms that are initially non-zero and satisfy certain symmetry properties. Notably, our findings also extend to the context of modular forms more broadly, as well as to a broader class of cusp forms that are categorized according to weight and degree.

In interior point methods (IPMs), where an iterative method is employed to solve a system of equations, speeding up convergence often involves introducing a preconditioner to enhance the efficiency of the iterative solver. However, determining when to stop the iterative process remains a major challenge. Standard termination criteria based on residuals or displacements may not be adequate, particularly in interior point methods. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a new preconditioner termination criterion that is derived from an analysis of the residual norm. Specifically, we begin by examining the relationship between the residual norm and interior point methods, before developing a data-dependent preconditioner. Furthermore, we establish a condition to determine when the preconditioner is effective and introduce an initial estimate for the preconditioner's quality. Lastly, we conduct numerical experiments to validate the effectiveness of our novel termination criterion.

We have derived the $O(\alpha_s^3)$ polarized spin-dependent Wilson coefficient $A_{gq}^{(3)}(x)$ of the parton distribution function, along with its color structure, which will enable us to obtain the transition matrix element $A_{gq}(N)$ when combined with $A_{gz}(N)$. The latter can be found in an earlier work referenced here. Using the AVN averaging procedure, we will be able to obtain an average value for $A_{gq}(N)$, which will allow us to obtain an estimate of the polarized parton distribution function $q^{\prime -}(x,N)$. The value of $A_{gq}(N)$ will also give us insight into the behavior of the polarized parton distribution functions $q^{\prime \pm}(x,N)$, which will be crucial in an upcoming analysis that will seek to explain the data suggesting the presence of a double-parton distribution function in neutron structure functions as reported in arXiv:2101.06218. The work will ultimately provide a detailed picture of how the transition matrix elements $A_{gz}(N)$ and $A_{gq}(N)$ evolve at large $N$ in the Variable Flavor Number Scheme.

Establishing a comprehensive knowledge base of previous AI failures is crucial for preventing the repetition of those mistakes. The AI Incident Repository, a database of significant AI failures, can provide valuable lessons for future developers, mitigating the likelihood of analogous incidents recurring. The repository's potential applications and benefits will be explored in this research, along with a proposed framework for establishing and maintaining the repository. Initially, we will analyze a set of prominent AI failures to identify common patterns and factors contributing to these failures.
